title: India's Forex Reserves Hit Record $729 Billion on NRI Deposit Surge
excerpt: The RBI's concessional swap facility drew nearly $73 billion in overseas inflows since June, pushing reserves past their February peak and prompting an early closure of the deposit window.
body:
• India's foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record $729.33 billion in the week ended August 21, surpassing the previous peak of $728.49 billion set in February.
  • The RBI's concessional swap facility drew nearly $73 billion in inflows since June 5, including $65 billion in NRI deposits, prompting an early closure of the scheme by August end.
  • Reserves have risen for eight consecutive weeks, gaining roughly $63 billion, but analysts warn the deposit-driven buildup may reverse once incentives expire.

India's foreign exchange reserves rose to an all-time high of $729.33 billion in the week ended August 21, Reserve Bank of India data showed on Friday, as a surge in overseas deposit inflows driven by the central bank's concessional swap program pushed the country's FX stockpile past its previous record.

The reserves jumped $12.42 billion from the prior week, marking the eighth straight weekly increase and a cumulative gain of about $63 billion over that stretch. The previous record of $728.49 billion was set in the week ended February 27.

RBI's Dollar Drive

The bulk of the increase traces to regulatory measures the RBI unveiled in June to bolster India's balance of payments. The central bank introduced discounted hedging facilities for overseas borrowings by state-run firms and banks, along with a free-of-cost hedging window for banks raising foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits.

Between June 5 and August 21, the RBI received nearly $73 billion under these schemes, with roughly $65 billion coming from FCNR-B deposits alone. Banks and public sector undertakings raised an additional $4.86 billion via overseas foreign currency borrowings and $2.59 billion through external commercial borrowings under the facility.

The sheer scale of inflows prompted the RBI to bring forward the closure of its deposit hedging facility by a month, moving the deadline to August 31 from the originally announced September 30. That accelerated timeline has, paradoxically, intensified the rush of deposits as banks scramble to lock in terms before the window shuts.

"The rise in FX reserves is a combination of RBI buying dollars during that week and the rest is revaluation gain. The dollar purchase is led by the FCNR-B swap window with banks pushing for deposits before the window closes."

— Gaura Sen Gupta, Chief Economist, IDFC First Bank

Breaking Down the Numbers

Foreign currency assets, the largest component of India's reserves, rose $9.48 billion during the week to $591.33 billion. Gold holdings gained $2.8 billion to reach $114.22 billion, extending a year-on-year increase of $29.22 billion that reflects the RBI's ongoing diversification into bullion. Special Drawing Rights with the IMF rose $112 million to $18.85 billion, while India's reserve tranche position edged up $26 million to $4.93 billion.

Since March-end 2026, the reserves have increased by $38.22 billion. On a year-on-year basis, the gain stands at $38.61 billion, underscoring a sustained improvement in India's external reserve position.

Rupee Implications and RBI Intervention

Despite the torrent of dollar inflows, the rupee's gains have been contained. Bankers said the RBI has been actively intervening in the foreign exchange market, absorbing dollars to prevent a sharp appreciation of the currency rather than letting the inflows translate directly into rupee strength.

Manoranjan Sharma, chief economist at Infomerics Ratings, noted that the reserve accumulation materially strengthens India's external buffer, giving the RBI capacity to smooth disorderly rupee depreciation, finance essential imports during oil-price or geopolitical shocks, and reassure foreign investors about the country's external-payment resilience.

Durability in Question

Analysts cautioned that the quality and durability of the reserve buildup matter as much as the headline number. The inflows are overwhelmingly deposit-driven, which means they raise India's external liabilities and could reverse when incentives expire or global yield dynamics shift.

"Instead of flowing into the open market to lift the rupee, most of it is landing straight into RBI's own reserves, with the central bank using this window to rebuild its war chest rather than let the dollars do the rupee's job."

— Amit Pabari, Managing Director, CR Forex Advisors

Sharma echoed the caution, noting that while the record stock improves near-term stability, it should not be taken as a sign that structural current-account vulnerabilities — especially India's dependence on oil imports — have disappeared.

With the concessional swap window closing at month-end, the coming weeks will test whether the reserves can hold near record levels without the policy-induced inflow tailwind. The RBI's reserve adequacy remains comfortable by standard metrics — covering over 10 months of merchandise imports and roughly 90.8% of external debt — but the transition from incentive-driven accumulation to organic reserve growth will be closely watched by markets.

In rupee terms, India's total foreign exchange reserves stood at ₹69.81 lakh crore as of August 21.
